mil3.2.5:1.2: “Venerable Nāgasena, is pleasant feeling skillful, unskillful, or indeterminate?”
mil3.2.5:1.3: “It may be skillful, Great King, it may be unskillful, and it may be indeterminate.”
mil3.2.5:1.4: “Venerable sir, if it is skillful it is not painful, and if it is painful it is not skillful; so there is no such thing as something skillful that is painful.”
mil3.2.5:1.5: “What do you think, Great King: suppose someone were to put a heated iron ball in one of a man’s hands and a cold lump of ice in the other. Would both of them burn him, Great King?”
mil3.2.5:1.7: “Great King, are both of them hot?”
mil3.2.5:1.9: “Then, Great King, are both of them cold?”
mil3.2.5:1.11: “Recognize the refutation: if what is hot burns, but both are not hot, then it does not hold.
mil3.2.5:1.12: If what is cold burns, but both are not cold, then it does not hold.
mil3.2.5:1.13: But why, Great King, do both of them burn, when both are not hot and both are not cold?
mil3.2.5:1.14: One is hot and one is cold, yet both of them burn; therefore it does not hold.”
mil3.2.5:1.15: “I am not able to converse with a debater like you. Please explain the meaning.”
mil3.2.5:1.16: Then the elder brought King Milinda to understand with a talk connected with the Abhidhamma—
mil3.2.5:2.1: “Great King, there are these six kinds of domestic happiness, six kinds of renunciate happiness, six kinds of domestic sadness, six kinds of renunciate sadness, six kinds of domestic equanimity, and six kinds of renunciate equanimity. These are the six sixes. Past feelings are of thirty-six kinds, future feelings are of thirty-six kinds, and present feelings are of thirty-six kinds. Gathered together and combined, they come to one hundred and eight feelings.”
